hypothesis: The valid baseline averages 0.135409 s over three measurements, but provides no per-size timings. For larger matrices, scalar row/column/reduction tiling should improve locality by traversing B and C contiguously and reusing their panels while preserving increasing-k accumulation for every output. This tests blocking without packing, scratch allocation, explicit SIMD, or OpenMP; its complete-call result, including memset, should be compared with repeated timings.

A four-row by four-column outer-product microkernel should improve arithmetic throughput on larger matrices by computing four output columns with vector operations and reusing each loaded B vector across four rows. Scalar tails preserve arbitrary dimensions; the controller must measure the target build before any speedup is claimed.

Static scheduling across disjoint output rows should avoid write races while keeping row writes contiguous. Both configurations call the same arithmetic row kernel; the serial path avoids OpenMP when the capped team is one. Each output is initialized by its accumulator and stored once, replacing the separate clear pass. Larger matrices may benefit from parallel rows, while small matrices may expose team-launch overhead; the candidate is unmeasured.

Refine selected parent a5c57a14961b47f9: retain its disjoint static row assignment and team cap, but accumulate eight adjacent output columns together. For each k this reads a contiguous segment of B while preserving increasing-k accumulation order per output; a scalar tail handles arbitrary widths. This isolates B-access locality from the parent’s scheduling mechanism. Expect lower one-thread end-to-end time at large sizes while retaining four-thread scaling. The hypothesis is falsified if neither one-thread large-size case improves by at least 5% versus the parent, or either four-thread case regresses by more than 5%; any correctness failure stops the candidate.

The only measured T1 candidate is the valid tiled program d4c32bef3fcc4618 (mean 0.022808 s versus baseline-e1 at 0.135409 s); catalog diversity is one distinct program. Since that candidate changed loop order and blocking together, this general, unblocked i-k-j control isolates loop interchange: each A[i,k] feeds contiguous B and C elements, while each output still accumulates k in increasing order after a full C initialization. I expect it to improve on the naive baseline and may recover much of the tiled result, but it may lose locality at larger n. Compare repeated complete-call timings at n=384 and 768 (thread arguments 1 and 4); stop promoting it if it is incorrect or, after repeated comparison, fails to beat the tiled candidate beyond observed timing variability.

This tests a wider 4x8 output tile against the earlier measured 4x4 vector kernel: two contiguous B-vector loads per k let each loaded A value contribute to eight outputs, while eight vector accumulators may increase register pressure. I expect any benefit to appear on larger matrices; this is not a claimed speedup. Stop if correctness or tail handling fails, or if target-build repeated timings do not show at least 5% improvement in one tested configuration without more than 5% regression in any other.

Retain selected parent a5c57a14961b47f9 and change only parallel row assignment from default contiguous static chunks to cyclic static,1. This tests whether interleaving equal-work rows changes four-thread behavior; the same row kernel runs in serial and parallel paths, the team remains capped at min(threads,n), and each thread owns whole disjoint rows. Expect one-thread timings to remain unchanged; four-thread large-size timings may change from row interleaving, though the parent’s contiguous chunks may be better for locality. Reject on any correctness failure, if either four-thread n=384 or n=768 regresses by more than 5%, or if neither improves by at least 5% versus the parent.

Retain selected parent a5c57a14961b47f9's capped static row scheduling and test a 16-column output tile in its shared serial/parallel row kernel. Each k step reuses one A value across 16 contiguous B values while each output sum retains increasing-k order; the scalar tail supports arbitrary dimensions. This tests the analyst's tile-width/register-pressure uncertainty against the measured 8-column dc2d5b7da77c4968 reference without claiming vectorization. Expect the 16-wide tile to improve at least one large 4-thread case if reduced loop overhead outweighs register costs. Falsify on any correctness failure, a greater-than-5% regression against the 8-wide reference in any 1-/4-thread large case, or failure to improve both 4-thread large cases by at least 5%.

The measured catalog has two distinct valid programs: unblocked i-k-j averaged 0.010488 s over three samples, versus 0.022808 s for 3D tiling; the baseline averaged 0.135409 s. This candidate tests a different B-reuse mechanism: group four output rows, traverse k in order, then apply each B row to all four rows with contiguous j access. It removes the previous full column/k tiling rather than adding packing. I expect possible benefit at larger n from reusing each B row across four outputs, but make no speedup claim. Compare repeated complete-call timings at n=384 and 768 against the measured i-k-j and tiled candidates; check a non-multiple size such as 385 and complete C overwrite. Stop if correctness or overwrite fails, or if repeats do not show an improvement beyond observed timing variation.

Unlike the recent whole-tile width comparisons, this tests whether the unresolved four-column tail is worth vectorizing: retain the 4x8 core, but use a 4x4 vector tile whenever at least four columns remain. Reject if arbitrary-size correctness or guards fail, if tail-bearing cases show no timing reduction, or if official target timings regress materially.

The measured T3 variants explored row scheduling and 8-/16-column arithmetic tiles; this candidate tests a different mechanism: static OpenMP scheduling across disjoint 16×32 output rectangles while keeping the scalar, increasing-k dot product identical in serial and parallel paths. Expect the four-thread run to improve over the one-thread run at n=384 and n=768, with no separate output-clear pass; this is a hypothesis, not a measured result. The catalog contains three distinct valid mechanisms, with measured overall means of 0.009722 s for the four-row reuse candidate, 0.010488 s for scalar i-k-j, and 0.022808 s for 3D tiling; none tests per-call packing. Recent measurements favor a 4x16 vector tile (0.006227 s) over an 8x4 tile (0.007052 s), but do not identify why. This tests an 8x8 tile with the same 16 live vector accumulators as 4x16: two contiguous B vectors are reused across eight rows. It may improve reuse and reduce tile-loop overhead, or lose to the wider column tile. The target build's repeated timings and correctness checks on arbitrary dimensions and tails can falsify the idea; no speedup is assumed.

Refine selected parent 15d05fc77a8f4b9b while retaining its 32-column tiles, increasing-k accumulation, direct output writes, and contiguous manual worker partition. Change each work item to a two-row tile so each B lane load updates two row accumulators; this tests B reuse with half the accumulator footprint of a four-row tile. The same kernel runs serially and in parallel, and team size is bounded by the positive threads argument and row-block count, using the actual OpenMP team for partitioning. The hypothesis is falsified by any correctness failure, less than 3% improvement in at least three of four complete-call comparisons at n=384/768 with 1/4 threads, or a regression over 3% in any comparison. Timings should include accumulator initialization, output stores, and OpenMP setup/fork-join.

Refine the selected scalar i-k-j parent by removing its separate C memset and seeding each output with the k=0 product, keeping subsequent accumulation in increasing k order. This tests whether eliminating a full output-initialization pass helps the complete call without changing its unblocked traversal or adding packing. The selected parent measured 0.010488 s; the measured eight-row full-width candidate was 0.009146 s and the packed-panel candidate 0.013917 s. The hypothesis is falsified if repeated complete-call timings, including seeding, fail to improve on the selected parent beyond timing variability. Validate edge sizes and complete C overwrite.

The catalog has 10 distinct measured programs, but shape changes have not guaranteed faster results: the 8x8 result was 0.005731 s, 4x16 was 0.006227 s, and the earlier K-lane reduction was 0.017130 s. The analyst also found 4x16 faster than 4x8 at n=384 but slower at n=768; spills remain unverified and prior measured sizes did not exercise tails. This base-derived 2x8 output-column SIMD kernel instead splits each reduction into even- and odd-k vector accumulators, combining them once after the loop. If the serial accumulation dependency is limiting throughput, the two chains may improve target-build time without a 16-accumulator output tile; lower row reuse and the final additions may instead hurt. Validate arbitrary dimensions and signed inputs, including n=389/773 if supported. Stop if correctness fails or repeated compatible target timings do not reproducibly beat the strongest measured reference; no improvement is assumed.

Refine the selected parent’s 2x4 full-k register microtile by widening it to 2x8. Reading eight contiguous B values per k may use cache lines more effectively and reduce repeated B sweeps across column tiles, while the larger accumulator set may increase register pressure. Test this with repeated complete-call timings against the selected parent (0.03977 s) and the measured 8-row control (0.00915 s); the hypothesis is falsified if the candidate does not improve repeatably. No speedup is assumed.

Refine selected parent d54e07efe56b4fb6, whose valid measured mean was 58.7 ms, by changing its column-at-a-time B transpose to disjoint, statically scheduled 32x32 transpose blocks. The existing increasing-k multiply_row arithmetic remains identical in serial and parallel paths, isolating transpose locality as the tested mechanism. Better source locality may reduce complete-call time; this is falsified by any correctness failure, no >=3% improvement over the parent in at least three of the four n=384/768 and 1/4-thread comparisons, or a >3% regression in any comparison. No speedup is claimed before controller measurement.

Refine the selected 4-row, full-k panel parent by widening only COLUMN_TILE from 128 to 256. At n=768 this halves the number of complete k sweeps per row group from six to three, potentially reducing repeated A loads, while increasing the active C panel from 2 KiB to 4 KiB. Test whether that tradeoff improves repeated complete-call timings, including memset, against the selected parent (aggregate mean 0.011244 s). The historical 8-row full-width result averaged 0.009146 s but differs in row grouping and initialization, so it is a reference rather than an isolated tile-width comparison. The hypothesis is falsified if the new panel width does not improve repeatably. Check edge tiles, arbitrary valid sizes, and complete C overwrite.

The measured 8x8 candidate is fastest in the supplied catalog (0.005731 s), while the analyst found that 4x16 versus 4x8 results vary by size and did not establish register spills. This base-derived experiment changes the reduction schedule rather than widening the tile: a 4x8 output-column SIMD kernel processes K in pairs while retaining eight vector accumulators. Pairing may reduce loop overhead and expose more load scheduling without increasing the accumulator count; temporary values or the narrower tile may offset that benefit. Test arbitrary sizes including residual cases such as n=389 and n=773 if supported. Stop on any correctness failure or if repeated compatible target timings do not reproducibly beat the measured reference; no improvement is assumed.

Test a distinct cache-blocked variant of row streaming: an 8-row by 256-column output tile reduces the active C panel relative to the measured 8-row full-width stream, potentially improving locality. The tradeoff is rescanning A and B for each column panel. Compare repeated complete-call timings, including k=0 output seeding, against the measured 8-row full-width result (0.009146 s) and scalar i-k-j reference (0.010488 s); the hypothesis is falsified if the smaller panel does not improve repeatably. Check edge tiles and complete C overwrite for arbitrary valid n.

Refine selected parent a5c57a14961b47f9 by retaining its increasing-k accumulation, direct complete output writes, and bounded static OpenMP work over disjoint rows, while replacing strided per-output dot products with an 8x8 k-outer microtile. The tile reuses each A value across columns and each contiguous B value across rows; the same worker runs serially or in parallel. This contrasts with recent 4x32 tile and schedule-granularity variants. The catalog has 26 distinct measured programs; c85d93e3257b46ec measured 3.959 ms versus 5f3531a8d8c14099 at 5.897 ms, while the selected parent measured 66.733 ms, so there is headroom but no measured causal claim for this tile. Test complete calls at 1 and 4 threads for n=384 and 768. The hypothesis is falsified by incorrect output, failure to improve by at least 3% in three of four comparisons against the selected parent, or a regression over 3% in any comparison.

The base uses r-c-k accumulation, which traverses B with a stride. This candidate tests recursive bisection of the row, column, and reduction dimensions until each leaf is at most 32 per dimension; its leaf uses i-k-j order with contiguous B and C column accesses. Unlike the recent fixed row streams and fixed-size panels, the recursive schedule bounds three-dimensional working sets without packing or scratch allocation. Full-call timings include output memset and recursion. If recursive locality helps beyond the measured 8-row full-width result (0.009146 s) or scalar i-k-j control (0.010488 s), repeated complete-call means should improve against those results; otherwise, or if any edge-size correctness or complete-overwrite check fails, the hypothesis is falsified. Reduction halves are visited in ascending order for each output.

The measured 8x8 SIMD tile is the strongest supplied candidate at 0.005731 s, while recent K-pair and split-chain variants measured 0.006439 s and 0.008508 s. This tests a different reduction mechanism: unroll the 8x8 tile's K loop by four while accumulating each output in its original sequential order and keeping the same 16 vector accumulators. Fewer loop-control operations and more load scheduling may help; code-size or register pressure may offset that. The target-build timing and correctness checks, including arbitrary tails and signed inputs, can falsify the hypothesis.

The fastest supplied measured variant, 88311d24594e453d, averaged 0.005652 s; the 8x8 result averaged 0.005731 s and the 4x16 result 0.006227 s. This experiment tests a 6x8 output tile with 12 live four-lane accumulators, rather than the recent 8x8 tile's 16 accumulators and K-loop unrolling. It may reduce register pressure while retaining reuse of each pair of contiguous B vectors across six output rows. The measurements do not establish that register spills caused prior differences, and the irregular row tile may instead cost more. The target build's repeated timings and correctness checks on arbitrary dimensions, tails, and signed inputs will falsify the hypothesis; no speedup is assumed.

Test an output-stationary scalar 4x4 tile: keep 16 partial sums in local scalars across the full increasing-k reduction, reuse four adjacent B values across four output rows, and store each full C tile once. This contrasts with recent row-streaming and cache-panel approaches by trading repeated C updates for repeated per-column-tile scans of k; it uses no explicit SIMD, OpenMP, packing, or scratch allocation. The complete call includes edge dot products and all C stores. Compare repeated timings and correctness, including odd sizes and complete overwrite, against the measured scalar i-k-j control (0.010488 s), 8-row full-width stream (0.009146 s), and 2x8 register tile (0.010811 s). The hypothesis is falsified if it does not improve repeatably over the scalar control or if any correctness/overwrite check fails; no speedup is assumed.

Refine selected parent 9917287caac04081 by retaining its 32-column row arithmetic, accumulator initialization, and direct complete output writes, but replace guided one-row scheduling with contiguous schedule(static) assignment. Rows have uniform work, so static assignment may reduce dispatch overhead, especially at four threads. The active-parallel-region serial fallback avoids creating a nested team, while num_threads(team) keeps the requested positive thread count as an upper bound; a request of one still uses the OpenMP path so its overhead is measured. Test complete calls, including OpenMP and accumulator/output-write costs, at 1 and 4 threads for n=384 and 768. The hypothesis is unsupported if the candidate is incorrect, fails to improve at least 3% in both four-thread cases, or regresses more than 3% in either one-thread case. No timing result is claimed before controller measurement.

This base exploration contrasts with recent 2- and 4-row tiled kernels: it assigns whole independent output rows, retains the original increasing-k dot-product order, and directly overwrites each output without first clearing C. The T3 catalog has 28 distinct measured programs; its listed best, c85d93e3257b46ec, measured 3.959 ms, while the cross-role Gm4 source f5182ece67de45eb measured 3.687 ms. The recent static-schedule variant bcf9ca118a474682 measured 7.362 ms, but its different kernel means these results do not isolate scheduling effects. Test complete calls at 1 and 4 threads for n=384 and 768, including the OpenMP region (also requested with one thread) and all output writes. The same row helper is used in both paths. The scaling hypothesis is falsified by incorrect output or if four threads are not at least 3% faster than one thread at both sizes; no speedup is claimed before controller measurement.

The selected 4x16 parent averaged 0.006227 s, while the measured 8x8 candidate with four-way K unrolling averaged 0.005652 s; those results confound tile shape with loop scheduling. This refinement keeps the parent's tile, accumulators, output paths, and arbitrary-size tails, but unrolls the main tile's K loop by four while preserving each output's sequential accumulation order. It tests whether fewer loop-control iterations and more instruction scheduling help without adding accumulators; code growth or register pressure may negate any benefit. Controller timings and correctness checks on signed inputs and tails will falsify the hypothesis; no speedup is assumed.

Test an iterative 32-row by 64-column output tile with 32-wide increasing-k panels. Unlike the recent full-width row stream, 4x4 register tile, and recursive 3D subdivision, this keeps a bounded C tile active across the full reduction while retaining contiguous i-k-j updates and reusing each B panel across rows. The intended tile working set is bounded without packing or scratch allocation; no cache-size fit or speedup is assumed. Compare repeated complete-call means, including C initialization, with scalar i-k-j (6ca0408f1c1f4a21: 0.010488 s) and the fastest measured 8-row stream (ab25b6d508044319: 0.009146 s). The hypothesis is falsified if the blocked candidate does not improve repeatably over those references or fails correctness/complete-overwrite checks on edge sizes.

The selected 2x8 parent uses separate even- and odd-k vector accumulators, then adds them when storing. This refinement keeps its tile, paired-k traversal, loads, and tail paths, but accumulates both contributions sequentially into four vectors instead of eight. If the extra live accumulators and final combination are costly, this may improve target timings; if the longer dependency chains dominate, it may regress. Repeated target-build timings against the parent and correctness checks on signed values and arbitrary tails can falsify the hypothesis; no speedup is assumed.

The base r-c-k loop visits B with a stride. The measured scalar i-k-j control (6ca0408f1c1f4a21: 0.010488 s) and 8-row stream (ab25b6d508044319: 0.009146 s) are faster than the measured packed-panel candidate 8eb932412b2a4849 (0.013917 s). That packed candidate packs within row groups. This tests whether packing each 32-by-128 B panel once and reusing it across all row groups amortizes that cost. The hypothesis is falsified if repeated complete-call timings, including C initialization and panel packing, do not improve over those references; no speedup is assumed.

Under the supplied protocol, the measured 8x8 SIMD kernel with K unrolled by four is fastest at 0.005652 s, while the measured 4x4 vector kernel is at 0.010744 s; these results do not isolate tile effects. This candidate uses a 4x8 tile with eight vector accumulators instead of sixteen, reusing each loaded B vector across four output rows and each A value across eight columns. Sequential K updates are explicitly unrolled by four. Repeated target-build timings can test whether the smaller live tile helps without sacrificing throughput; correctness checks across signed inputs and dimensions with column, row, and K tails can falsify the implementation. No speedup is assumed.

Refine selected parent 6be9fa3531524703 by retaining its 32-column tile arithmetic and direct complete output writes, but replace cyclic schedule(static,1) assignment with default contiguous schedule(static) over the collapsed row/tile iteration space. Contiguous assignment may reduce scheduling and cache-line contention between workers. The catalog has 29 distinct programs; its fastest listed candidate c85d93e3257b46ec measured 3.959 ms, but changed tile shape as well, so it does not isolate scheduling. Test complete calls at 1 and 4 requested threads for n=384 and 768; positive requests, including one, enter OpenMP, and the team remains bounded by threads and available tiles. The hypothesis is falsified by incorrect output or if the 4-thread mean does not improve at least 3% over the selected parent in either large-size case. No speedup or measured 1-/4-thread result is claimed here.

Refine selected parent 15d05fc77a8f4b9b: retain its 32-column tiles, increasing-k accumulation, direct output writes, and contiguous manual partition, but make each work item four rows by 32 columns so each loaded B value updates four row accumulators. This differs from the recent one-row scheduling changes and the earlier two-row candidate; the measured four-row candidate c85d93e3257b46ec motivates testing row reuse, but its different scheduling does not isolate the effect. Test full calls at 1 and 4 requested threads for n=384 and 768. For every positive request, including one, enter OpenMP and cap the team by the row-block count and requested threads; partition using the actual team size and use the serial helper path for nested calls. The hypothesis is falsified by incorrect output, failure to improve at least 3% over the selected parent in both four-thread large-size comparisons, or more than 3% regression in either one-thread comparison. Accumulator initialization, output stores, and OpenMP overhead remain in the timed call; no separate C clear or speedup is claimed.

The best measured 8x8 SIMD candidate (88311d24594e453d, 0.005652 s) traverses row tiles outside column tiles. This experiment retains its 8x8 vector kernel and four-way K unrolling but reverses that outer tile order, processing each 8-column B strip across row tiles before moving on. If cache reuse of that strip outweighs less row-wise output locality, target-build timings should improve; otherwise they should regress. Arbitrary row, column, and K tails remain scalar-correct. No speedup is assumed.

Refine the selected 2x4 output-stationary kernel by changing only the column tile width to six. At n=768 this reduces full-column tiles per two-row group from 192 to 128 and reuses each loaded A pair across six contiguous B values, while increasing the tile to 12 accumulators. This tests the tradeoff between fewer K-loop traversals and accumulator pressure; compare repeated complete-call timings, including edge handling, with the selected parent (0.03977 s) and measured 2x8 alternative (0.01081 s). No speedup is assumed.

Refine selected parent a5c57a14961b47f9 by retaining disjoint static row ownership and a runtime-bounded team, while changing its strided per-output dot products to k-outer contiguous row updates with SIMD over columns. Each output starts at zero once and accumulates k in increasing order. Test complete calls, including that initialization and OpenMP overhead, at 1 and 4 requested threads for n=384 and 768. The hypothesis is falsified by incorrect output, failure to improve the comparable 4-thread parent timings at either size, or failure of 4 threads to outperform 1 at either size. No candidate measurement is claimed.

The fastest measured reference uses an 8x8 tile, four-way sequential K unrolling, and 16 four-lane accumulators (88311d24594e453d, 0.005652 s). This candidate keeps the tile and unroll but uses eight AVX eight-lane accumulators and one 8-float B load per K step instead of two 4-float loads. If wider vectors reduce instruction and load overhead, repeated target-build timings should improve; AVX overhead, register effects, or target frequency behavior could instead erase the benefit. Runtime feature dispatch and scalar row, column, and K tails make the path safe for arbitrary dimensions and non-AVX CPUs. The controller's correctness checks and measurements can falsify the hypothesis; no speedup is assumed.

The selected recursive parent bisects k as well as the output dimensions, so it returns to output tiles across multiple reduction leaves. This refinement keeps its recursive row/column tiling and i-k-j leaf order but visits the full k range in ascending order within each leaf. It tests whether avoiding k-recursion improves tile locality or reduces dispatch overhead. Compare repeated complete-call timings, including C initialization, with the selected parent (0.049732 s) and the measured scalar i-k-j and 8-row stream controls (0.010488 s and 0.009146 s). The hypothesis is falsified if the candidate does not improve repeatably over its parent or fails correctness/complete-overwrite checks, including odd edge sizes such as n=385; no speedup is assumed.

Refine selected parent f752fae93dc442cb while retaining its exact per-output arithmetic order and row helper. Bypass the one-worker OpenMP loop for requests with an effective team of one, and replace the parallel-for scheduler with explicit contiguous row ranges based on the actual bounded team size. This tests whether one-thread runtime overhead and loop scheduling cost matter without changing the arithmetic. The hypothesis is falsified by any correctness failure, less than 3% improvement in complete-call times at 1 requested thread for both n=384 and n=768, or a regression above 3% at 4 requested threads for either size. No speedup is claimed before measurement.

Retain selected parent c67dd9aabae34343's 4-row by 64-column arithmetic, increasing-k accumulation, SIMD inner loop, and direct output writes, but assign whole row blocks rather than flattened row-block/column-tile tasks. Each worker will visit all column tiles for its owned row block, reducing scheduled units by the number of column tiles (6 at n=384 and 12 at n=768), while keeping the arithmetic helper identical in serial and parallel paths. This may reduce scheduling and flattening overhead and strengthen row locality; coarser work assignment could instead hurt balance. Falsify the hypothesis on any correctness failure, if 4-thread complete-call time fails to improve by at least 3% over the parent at both n=384 and n=768, or if either 1-thread comparison regresses by more than 3%. Measure full calls at 1 and 4 requested threads, including OpenMP and accumulator initialization/output stores; no separate C clear is performed and no speedup is claimed before measurement.

The measured 8x8 AVX candidate 1bf2f6d26b35450b averaged 0.003631 s and used separate vector multiply/add operations. This experiment keeps an 8x8 tile, eight row accumulators, and four-way K unrolling, but uses runtime-dispatched AVX+FMA to contract each contribution into one vector operation. If the target supports FMA and its instruction throughput helps, the measured mean should beat that reference; if it does not, timings may be unchanged or worse. Stop this line if correctness fails or the target-build result does not reproducibly beat the reference.

The selected parent (6be9fa3531524703; measured mean 0.007706 s) schedules flattened row/tile tasks with static,1, so multiple workers handle tiles of each row. Assigning whole rows with static scheduling may improve per-row output locality and reduce scheduled iterations, while leaving its 1x32 arithmetic helper unchanged in both serial and parallel paths. Unlike recent 3116f3f2e35b4b7c, which also changed to a 4x64 SIMD kernel, this isolates row ownership around the selected parent's arithmetic. Compare full-call timings at 1 and 4 requested threads for n=384 and 768, including any OpenMP and accumulator/output costs. Falsify on incorrect output, failure to improve the parent's 4-thread time at both large sizes, or a greater than 3% regression in either 1-thread comparison; no speedup is claimed before measurement.

Le catalogue compte 20 programmes T2 mesurés, tous distincts et valides. Le meilleur résultat observé est le 8×8 AVX/FMA à 0,003615 s; le 4×16 antérieur à vecteurs de quatre voies a pris 0,006227 s, mais cette comparaison confond la forme de tuile et la largeur SIMD. Je teste donc une tuile 4×16 AVX/FMA avec huit accumulateurs YMM, le même nombre que le 8×8 AVX, et un déroulage K par quatre. Elle réutilise deux vecteurs B sur quatre lignes et chaque valeur A sur deux vecteurs. Si la réutilisation accrue de A et la réduction des itérations de colonnes compensent les deux chargements de B, les mesures cible devraient battre le 8×8; sinon elles devraient régresser. Arrêter en cas d’erreur de correction ou si aucune amélioration reproductible n’apparaît.

The measured 4x32 candidate c85 (mean 0.003959 s) is faster than the selected 1x32 parent (0.011306 s), but does not isolate tile shape from scheduling. Test a 2x64 tile with the same 128 accumulator elements as 4x32: it should halve the number of column tiles while reusing each B value across two rows, though reduced row reuse or wider-lane costs may offset that. Compare complete calls at 1 and 4 requested threads for n=384 and 768, including accumulator initialization, output stores, and OpenMP overhead. The hypothesis is falsified by incorrect output, failure to improve 4-thread time by at least 3% over the selected parent at either size, or a 1-thread regression above 3% at either size; no speedup is claimed before measurement.

Le meilleur résultat T2 observé est le microkernel AVX/FMA 8×8 (bca5b197f6444d4a, 0,003615 s); le récent 4×16 mesuré à 0,003919 s ne prouve pas qu’une plus grande tuile aide. Je garde la largeur SIMD de huit colonnes et le déroulage K par quatre, mais teste une tuile 12×8 : chaque vecteur B sert à douze lignes plutôt qu’à huit. Si l’amortissement des chargements compense les douze accumulateurs et leur pression sur les registres, les mesures répétées cible devraient battre le 8×8; sinon, elles devraient stagner ou régresser. Le calcul scalaire couvre toutes les dimensions et queues.

The base performs the same scalar r-c-k dot product serially. Assigning each complete, disjoint output row to a static OpenMP iteration should reduce full-call time at four requested threads for large dimensions while preserving each output's accumulation order. This is materially different from recent tiled experiments: it keeps the base arithmetic kernel and isolates row scheduling, with no accumulator tiles or k-outer SIMD. Positive requests, including one, enter the OpenMP path so the comparison includes region overhead; the team is capped by the request, row count, and runtime limit. The hypothesis is falsified by any correctness failure or if the complete 4-thread call is not faster than the 1-thread call at n=384 and n=768. No speedup is claimed before measurement.

The catalog contains 22 distinct valid T2 programs, but recent AVX tile-size variants are clustered near the 8×8 AVX/FMA result (0.003615 s; 12×8 took 0.003621 s, while 4×16 took 0.003919 s). Rather than make another small explicit-SIMD tile change, this experiment tests cache-blocked i-k-j rank-1 updates with a contiguous, compiler-vectorizable column loop. Blocking may make repeated B and C accesses more cache-friendly than the measured unblocked i-k-j variant (0.010414 s) while avoiding a target-specific ISA path. Repeated target-build timings can falsify the hypothesis if the compiler does not vectorize the inner loop or the blocking overhead outweighs reuse.

The selected guided row kernel currently opens an OpenMP region even when the effective team has only one thread. Reusing the identical row/tile arithmetic serially when team <= 1, and falling back to serial inside an active parallel region, should remove unnecessary one-thread region overhead and prevent nested teams while retaining guided scheduling for larger teams. The falsifiable test is full-call timing at 1 and 4 requested threads, including tile accumulator initialization, output stores, and any OpenMP costs, at representative large sizes; the hypothesis is unsupported if 1-thread timings do not improve or 4-thread timings regress, and correctness must hold for all valid dimensions.

The selected parent opens an OpenMP region for requests above one thread even when n is smaller than its 32-column tile, where the tile has little work. Bypassing that region for n < 32 should lower complete-call time for small matrices; the active-region guard also avoids nested teams. The same tile arithmetic and direct output writes remain in serial and parallel paths. Test full calls at 1 and 4 requested threads for n=17, 32, 384, and 768, including OpenMP and initialization costs. The small-size hypothesis is falsified if the 4-thread n=17 call does not improve over the parent; reject the dispatch change if it causes a greater than 2% 4-thread regression at n>=32 or any correctness failure. No candidate speedup is claimed before measurement.

The measured 8×8 AVX/FMA candidate is fastest among the supplied T2 results at about 3.615 ms, while the 12×8 and 4×16 variants did not improve on it. This experiment tests a different mechanism rather than another tile-size change: a 4×8 AVX tile maintains separate even- and odd-K FMA accumulators for each row, aiming to shorten accumulation dependency chains while keeping eight vector accumulators total and reusing each B vector across four rows. The smaller row tile and altered reduction order could offset that benefit. Compare repeated actual-target timings against the 8×8 AVX/FMA result; if the split-chain kernel does not improve reproducibly, the dependency-chain assumption is falsified.
